title: Probability & Bayes' Rule
html:
Logic says a sentence is true, false or unknown. Real agents need degrees of belief: a toothache makes a cavity likely, not certain. Probability theory is the calculus of belief, and Bayes' rule is how an agent updates it when evidence arrives.

Why logic isn't enough

A rule like Toothache ⇒ Cavity is wrong (gum disease, abscesses…), and listing every exception fails for three reasons: laziness (too many rules), theoretical ignorance (medicine has no complete theory) and practical ignorance (not every test has been run). Probabilities summarise all of that uncertainty.

The rules you need

RuleFormula
Conditional probabilityP(a | b) = P(a ∧ b) / P(b)
Product ruleP(a ∧ b) = P(a | b) · P(b)
Marginalisation (sum out)P(a) = Σ_b P(a, b)
IndependenceP(a | b) = P(a) ⇔ P(a ∧ b) = P(a)·P(b)
Conditional independenceP(a ∧ b | c) = P(a | c) · P(b | c)
Bayes' ruleP(cause | effect) = P(effect | cause) · P(cause) / P(effect)

With the full joint distribution, any question is answered by summing entries. The textbook dentist domain (Toothache, Cavity, the probe Catches):

Watch out

The full joint grows as 2ⁿ for n Boolean variables — 2³⁰ ≈ a billion numbers for just 30 symptoms. Independence and conditional independence (Bayesian networks, next topic) are what make probabilistic reasoning tractable.

Bayes' rule and the base-rate fallacy

P(D | +) = P(+ | D) · P(D) / [ P(+ | D) · P(D) + P(+ | ¬D) · P(¬D) ]
Key point

Most positives come from the 99% of healthy people. Ignoring the prior (the base rate) is the base-rate fallacy — a favourite interview question. Bayes' rule is also diagnostic reasoning: we usually know P(effect | cause) (how a disease causes symptoms) and want P(cause | effect).

Naive Bayes

Assume every effect is conditionally independent given the cause: P(Cause, e₁…eₙ) = P(Cause) · Π P(eᵢ | Cause). Wrong in detail, but it needs only O(n) numbers and works remarkably well for text classification:

The Machine Learning notes cover naive Bayes as a classifier (variants, evaluation); here it matters as the simplest Bayesian network — one cause with independent effects.

State Bayes' rule and explain each term.

P(H | E) = P(E | H) · P(H) / P(E). P(H) is the prior belief in the hypothesis, P(E | H) the likelihood of the evidence if H is true, P(E) the total probability of the evidence (a normaliser), and P(H | E) the posterior belief after seeing the evidence.

A test is 90% sensitive with a 9% false-positive rate; the disease affects 1%. You test positive — what's the probability you have it?

About 9%: 0.9 × 0.01 / (0.9 × 0.01 + 0.09 × 0.99) ≈ 0.092. The low base rate means false positives from healthy people outnumber true positives.

Why is naive Bayes called naive?

It assumes all features are conditionally independent given the class, which is rarely true (words in an email are correlated). The assumption makes it fast and data-efficient, and classification often stays accurate even when the probabilities themselves are poorly calibrated.
